svg.aria-label: Diagram: access, ID and refresh tokens on Microsoft Entra, showing which party each token is intended for and who validates it, the deliberately randomised 60 to 90 minute access token lifetime, the refresh token revocation table in which most conditions leave tokens alive, the difference between the pairwise sub claim and the shared oid claim, and the token lifetime policy properties retired on 30 January 2021
svg.title: Three tokens, three jobs, and almost every token bug is a job swap
svg.text: Three tokens, three jobs. Almost every token bug is a job swap.
And the lifetimes are not the round numbers everyone codes against — the variation is deliberate, and it is not for your benefit.
Who each token is for, and who is allowed to read it
TOKEN
INTENDED FOR
WHO VALIDATES IT
DEFAULT LIFETIME
Access token
the API named in its aud claim
the resource server, never the client
60–90 min, randomised
ID token
your own client, as proof of sign-in
confidential clients only
one hour
Refresh token
Entra alone — it is encrypted
nobody else can read it at all
90 days; 24 h for a SPA
Revocation, read honestly: most of the table says “Stays alive”
Password expires
stays alive in every one of the five token classes
User changes password, or does SSPR
only password-based tokens go; the confidential client keeps its own
Admin resets password — Azure portal
confidential client token stays alive
Admin resets password — Entra or M365 admin centre
that one is revoked. Same act, different console, different outcome.
User or admin revokes refresh tokens
everything is revoked — the only row that is unambiguous
Identify a user: sub is pairwise, oid is not
sub
“a pairwise identifier and is unique to an
application ID” — two of your own apps get
two different values for the same person
oid
immutable, and the same across apps — but
different in every tenant, by design
email, preferred_username, name
all mutable, all reusable. “Your application mustn’t use
human-readable data to identify a user.”
Share data across services on oid + tid. Nothing else.
What you can still configure, and what is ignored
AccessTokenLifetime
10 minutes to 23:59:59. Despite the name it also
governs ID tokens and SAML2 tokens.
“As of January 30, 2021, refresh and session token
lifetimes are no longer configurable through token
lifetime policies.” Existing ones are not an error:
“those properties are ignored.”
And the precedence runs the wrong way round: an
organization-level policy beats an application-level
one. There is no portal UI for any of it.
Why the access token lifetime is a random number
Entra assigns “a random value ranging between 60-90 minutes (75 minutes on average)”, and says why: “The variation improves service
resilience by spreading access token demand over a time, which prevents hourly spikes in traffic to Microsoft Entra ID.” That is a
capacity decision made in Microsoft’s interest that lands in your app’s timing. With sign-in frequency set to one hour, the real gap
between credential prompts “occurs anywhere between 1 hour to 2.5 hours”. Where client and resource both support CAE it goes the
other way entirely, extending “to 24-28 hours, when it is safe to do so” — long tokens, revoked in near real time instead.
The client never needs to parse any of this: the token response carries the expiry and the scopes, “which allows the application to do
intelligent caching of access tokens without having to parse the access token itself”.
Sources: Access tokens, ID tokens, Refresh tokens, the ID token claims reference and Configurable token lifetimes, on Microsoft Learn.
